name: Lake Abbe
blurb: A salt lake in the Afar rift where flamingos, gazelles and scavengers share scarce water.

tip.title: Cut the Awash River
tip.text: Almost all of the lake's water arrives via the Awash. Lower it and watch the algae, then the flamingos, and the scavengers that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Intense, nearly year-round sun drives plant growth and also the heat and evaporation that make the basin so dry.

nodes.name: Scarce seasonal rain
nodes.desc: Only roughly 100 to 200 mm of rain falls a year in the Afar region, so brief wadi flows matter for plants and animals.

nodes.name: Awash River inflow
nodes.desc: The Awash is the lake's main source of water. It has no outflow, so salts build up and the level swings with river supply.

nodes.name: Mineral soils and salts
nodes.desc: Volcanic, mineral-rich ground and salt flats around the lake. Little organic matter builds up in the heat.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, algae and carcasses where moisture allows, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Spirulina and other cyanobacteria
nodes.desc: Blue-green algae that thrive in very alkaline, salty lakes and are the main food of lesser flamingos. Their presence here is inferred from flamingo use of the lake.

nodes.name: Umbrella thorn acacia
nodes.desc: Flat-topped thorny tree of dry wadis and lowlands in Djibouti. Its leaves and pods feed browsers.

nodes.name: Buffel grass
nodes.desc: Drought-tolerant bunch grass of wadis and lowland plains, grazed when rain brings new growth.

nodes.name: Desert panic grass
nodes.desc: Tough perennial desert grass listed among the plants of Djibouti's wadis and lowlands.

nodes.name: Lesser flamingo
nodes.desc: Filters spirulina, other algae and tiny invertebrates from alkaline lakes with its deep bill. Flamingos are the wildlife noted at Lake Abbe.

nodes.name: Desert locust
nodes.desc: Eats leaves, shoots and seeds of many plants, roughly its body weight daily, and can form huge swarms after rains.

nodes.name: Dorcas gazelle
nodes.desc: Small gazelle that mostly eats acacia leaves, flowers and pods plus desert bushes. Gets most of its water from succulents.

nodes.name: Soemmerring's gazelle
nodes.desc: One of the most commonly recorded antelopes of Djibouti's dry country, helped by the hunting ban of the early 1970s.

nodes.name: Common warthog
nodes.desc: Pig-like grazer that also digs for roots; recorded in the area and listed as vulnerable in Djibouti.

nodes.name: Hamadryas baboon
nodes.desc: Omnivore eating grasses, seeds, fruit, acacia leaves, insects and small animals. Depends on a few permanent waterholes in the dry season.

nodes.name: Somali wild ass
nodes.desc: Critically endangered wild ass of the Horn of Africa that grazes in the Afar region; foals begin grazing within two weeks.

nodes.name: Ragazzi's fan-footed gecko
nodes.desc: Rock-dwelling gecko recorded near the lake that hunts small insects such as locusts and other arthropods.

nodes.name: African golden wolf
nodes.desc: Eats invertebrates, rodents, reptiles and small mammals up to gazelle fawns, plus carrion and fruit. Recorded eating donkeys here.

nodes.name: Rüppell's vulture
nodes.desc: Strict carrion feeder that travels over 100 km from its nest and gathers at carcasses with other vultures.

nodes.name: Striped hyena
nodes.desc: Mainly a scavenger of ungulate carcasses that also kills smaller animals and eats fruit. A natural predator of hamadryas baboons.
